321.quote_or_event: “The Arhats and Bhagavats of the past, present, and future, all say thus, speak thus, declare thus, explain thus: all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away. This is the pure, unchangeable, eternal law…”
321.explanation: The lecture of the Ācārāṅga called 'Righteousness' defines the eternal law of all the Jinas as non-injury to every living being.
321.tie_back: Asked what aram is, Valluvar answers 'not killing'; the Ācārāṅga likewise makes non-killing the very definition of the eternal dharma.
321.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.4.1.1–2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
321._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near one-to-one match on non-killing as the essence of righteousness, though the Kural's second clause (killing brings all other evils) is not stated here.

322.quote_or_event: Jain householder ethics joins sharing food with protecting life: the vow of sharing with guests (atithi-saṃvibhāga) is one of the householder's supplementary vows, and the classical Jain list of gifts places the gift of food (āhāra-dāna) alongside the gift of fearlessness or protection of life (abhaya-dāna).
322.explanation: For the Jain layperson, generosity with food and active protection of living beings are the positive counterparts of the vow of non-violence.
322.tie_back: The Kural ranks sharing one's food and protecting many lives as the chief of all virtues; Jain lay ethics pairs exactly these two, food-giving and life-protecting, as core duties.
322.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.21 (Digambara numbering; atithi-saṃvibhāga vow), with the traditional fourfold dāna scheme in later Jain śrāvakācāra literature
322._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of Jain lay doctrine, not verified against a live text in this session; the sūtra number follows the Digambara recension (7.16 in the Śvetāmbara recension).

323.quote_or_event: In the Jain list of the five great vows (mahāvratas) taken by monks and the five lesser vows (aṇuvratas) of laypeople, the vow of non-killing (ahiṃsā) always stands first and the vow of truthfulness (satya) second, as in the account of Mahāvīra's five great vows and their clauses.
323.explanation: Jainism orders its vows with non-injury at the head and abstention from falsehood immediately after it.
323.tie_back: Valluvar ranks non-killing as the peerless good with not-lying following close behind; the Jain sequence of vows gives precisely this order.
323.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra II.15 (the five great vows; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
323._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested doctrinal ordering, not quoted; the match is structural (the same ranking) rather than an explicit statement that truth is second in value.

324.quote_or_event: “A wise man should study them with all means of philosophical research. All beings hate pains; therefore one should not kill them. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything.”
324.explanation: In the lecture titled 'The Path', the Sūtrakṛtāṅga answers 'what is the path?' by enumerating all classes of living beings and concluding that the essence of wisdom is to kill nothing.
324.tie_back: The Kural defines the good path as the way that takes thought to kill nothing at all; Mahāvīra's 'Path' lecture likewise makes 'not to kill anything' its core after careful study of every form of life.
324._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the framing as 'the Path' and the scope 'anything' match the Kural very closely.

325.quote_or_event: “He who thoroughly knows living beings, whether they move or not, and does not injure them in any of the three ways, him we call a Brâhmana.”
325.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that the true holy man is defined not by birth or ritual but by knowing all living beings and injuring none in thought, word or act.
325.tie_back: Valluvar places at the head of all renunciants the one who dreads killing; the Uttarādhyayana likewise makes non-injury the mark of the true ascetic.
325._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's 'Brâhmana' rendered here without diacritic italics); a strong thematic fit, though the verse defines the true ascetic rather than ranking him above other renunciants.

326.quote_or_event: “He should cease to injure living beings whether they move or not, on high, below, and on earth. For this has been called the Nirvâna, which consists in peace.”
326.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga identifies complete cessation of injury with nirvāṇa, the deathless peace beyond the round of births.
326.tie_back: The Kural says death will not overtake the one who lives by non-killing; the Jain text gives a spiritual version, equating non-injury with the peace of liberation, beyond death's reach.
326._accuracy_note: Verified on sacred-texts.com; only a partial match, since Jainism does not promise physical escape from death (Ācārāṅga I.2.3.4 says 'nothing is inaccessible for death'), so the fit holds only on the liberation reading of the Kural.

327.quote_or_event: The monk Dharmaruci was given a bitter, poisonous gourd dish as alms by the Brahmin woman Nāgaśrī. Told by his teacher to discard it, he saw ants die after tasting a single drop, and rather than let more creatures perish he ate the whole dish himself and died.
327.explanation: This celebrated canonical story presents a monk who gave up his own life rather than cause the death of even tiny creatures.
327.tie_back: Valluvar says one must not take another's precious life even at the cost of one's own; Dharmaruci literally chose his own death over killing ants.
327.source: Jñātādharmakathāṅga, ch. 16 (Draupadī's former birth as Nāgaśrī); retold in 'Dharmaruchi Muni', Jain stories, jainworld.com
327._accuracy_note: Paraphrased narrative; story confirmed on jainworld.com via web search, but the canonical chapter text itself was not read in this session.

328.quote_or_event: “The binding of animals (to the sacrificial pole), all the Vêdas, and sacrifices, being causes of sin, cannot save the sinner; for his works (or Karman) are very powerful.”
328.explanation: Jayaghosha rejects animal sacrifice: whatever rewards it promises, ritual killing is a cause of sin and binds the sacrificer with karma.
328.tie_back: Parimelazhagar reads the Kural as condemning the 'great gain' promised by sacrificial killing; this verse makes the same anti-sacrificial judgement from the Jain canon.
328._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit on the sacrificial reading, though the Kural's general claim (any gain through killing is base) is broader than the sacrifice context.

329.quote_or_event: “Be without fear, O king; but grant safety to others also; in this transient world of living beings, why are you addicted to cruelty?”
329.explanation: King Sañjaya, out hunting, killed a frightened deer and then met the monk Gardabhāli, who rebuked his habit of killing; the king renounced his throne.
329.tie_back: The Kural brands those who make killing their pursuit as doers of base deeds; the monk names the hunting king's killing 'cruelty' and turns him from it.
329.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 18.2 and 18.11 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
329._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good thematic fit, though it concerns a king's hunting rather than people whose livelihood is killing, and the language is rebuke rather than the Kural's verdict of baseness.

330.quote_or_event: “Carefully conducting himself, he should mind this: blindness, deafness, dumbness, one-eyedness, hunchbackedness, blackness, variety of colour (he will always experience); because of his carelessness he is born in many births, he experiences various feelings.”
330.explanation: The Ācārāṅga teaches that bodily afflictions in later births follow from careless conduct, which in Jain terms (pramāda) is the root of injury to living beings.
330.tie_back: The Kural traces diseased bodies and wretched lives to past killing; the Ācārāṅga likewise attributes bodily defects in rebirth to careless, injurious conduct.
330.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.3.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
330._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the karmic causation of bodily affliction matches, but the verse speaks of carelessness generally rather than killing specifically; Jacobi's 'blackness' reflects his period's wording.
